title: Churn model scores 96% in testing, barely beats a coin flip in production

hints.title: Where to look
hints.body: Open `src/train.py` and read every column name in `build_features()`. Ask yourself for each feature: **"Would I know this value at the moment I need to predict whether a customer will churn?"** One of the columns encodes something that can only be known *after* the customer has already churned.

hints.title: The concept
hints.body: This is **target leakage** (a form of data leakage). The column `refund_issued` is populated by the billing system only *after* a customer cancels their account — meaning at prediction time (for active customers), it is always `0`. The model learns that `refund_issued = 1` ≈ churned, achieving 96% accuracy in cross-validation but failing completely in production where every live customer has `refund_issued = 0`.

hints.title: The fix approach
hints.body:
In `build_features()`, drop the leaky column before returning the feature matrix:
```python
features = features.drop(columns=["refund_issued"])
```
This is the single-line fix. More broadly, always audit your features for post-label information: columns filled by downstream business processes (refunds, cancellation reasons, support tickets filed after churn) are common sources of leakage. A useful sanity check is to look at feature importances — a leaky feature will have implausibly high importance.

badPatches.title: Log-Transforming Leaky Column Instead of Dropping
badPatches.summary: 60/100 — passes visible tests (60/60), fails H1 (production simulation) and H2 (feature inspection)
